result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.effective_size()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Calculate Burt's effective size of every node's network. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L37476-L37546){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.effective_size( weighted=None, attr_name=None, return_dict=False, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Effective size](/assets/graphs/effective-size.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="The shared seven-node strip of triangles with a tail, shaded by Burt's effective size: the number of contacts minus how redundant they are with one another. Hub C has four contacts that partly know each other and scores 2.50, the bridge E 2.33, and F, whose two contacts E and G are unlinked, a full 2.00; A and G score 1.00." width="100%"} Effective size (Burt, 1992) is the number of a node's contacts, discounted for redundancy: contacts who are tied to one another bring overlapping information and count for less. A node whose contacts all know each other has an effective size close to 1; a broker whose contacts are strangers to one another has an effective size equal to its degree. It is the classic measure of *structural holes*, the gaps in a network that a well-placed broker can bridge. For the complementary measure of how constrained a node is, see `constraint()`. For an unweighted undirected graph this is `degree - 2t / degree`, where `t` is the number of ties among the node's contacts. Weighted and directed graphs use Burt's general formula, with tie strengths as proportions of each node's total. Self-loops are ignored. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [weighted]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Whether to use edge weights as tie strengths. If `None` (default), follows the graph. [attr_name]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the node attribute to store scores in. If `None` (default), uses `"effective_size"`. [return_dict]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, returns a dictionary instead of self. If `False` (default), stores the scores as a node attribute and returns self for chaining. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Union[dict[int, float | None], Graph]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_dict=` is `True`: a dictionary mapping node IDs to effective sizes (`None` for nodes without contacts). If `return_dict=` is `False` (default): returns self. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} The broker B links three contacts who do not know one another and keeps its full effective size of 3, while C, whose two contacts know each other, has only 1: ::: {#218706eb .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["B", "A", "X", "Y", "C", "D", "E"]) .add_edges([("B", "A"), ("B", "X"), ("B", "Y"), ("C", "D"), ("C", "E"), ("D", "E")]) ) sizes = graph.effective_size(return_dict=True) {graph.get_label_from_id(n): s for n, s in sorted(sizes.items())} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {'B': 3.0, 'A': 1.0, 'X': 1.0, 'Y': 1.0, 'C': 1.0, 'D': 1.0, 'E': 1.0} ``` ::: ::: ## Notes {.doc-notes} On weighted graphs NetworkX's `effective_size()` takes a sparse-matrix shortcut whose results disagree with its own per-node formula; EdgeCase follows the formula (and NetworkX's result when it is called with an explicit `nodes=` list). On directed graphs NetworkX returns NaN for any node without outgoing edges; EdgeCase counts incoming ties as contacts too and returns `None` only for nodes with no ties at all.
